utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone. General, good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you - we mentioned this during our conversation - you had experience in other civil wars; is that correct? Can you please tell us, which wars are these?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first experience with the UN was in Cyprus in the mid-1980s. I was back in Bosnia in 1997, and I've also spent nine months in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any similarities in these civil conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only similarity I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, General. I don't see any relevance, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have faith, Your Honours. You will see that there is relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't hear the interpretation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the similarities were between these three civil conflicts. I can repeat. I wanted to ask you, General, if you could tell us if you saw any similarities or differences in all of these conflicts, from the point of view of the fate of civilians, from the position of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I told you to move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to say that shielding behind civilians in those environments, in particular in Afghanistan, was quite a prominent feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can make your submission later on. Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would now like to go through a topic now, or actually I can continue with what we were doing yesterday regarding proportionality, and especially in relation to our relationship, meaning the parties to the conflict, and UNPROFOR, and the NATO bombing. I would like to ask to look at a document now, please. There was a crisis about Gorazde, but in autumn, September 1994, there was also a crisis in Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Gorazde and Sarajevo in 1994, but -- I remember them, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D2623, please. 1D2623, please. I don't know if we have a translation. This is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to the Commands of the Sarajevo Romanija, Hercegovac and Drina Corps, and the document describes the conduct of our opponents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you recall at the time, the exclusion zone was in force which applied to heavy weaponry all around Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'm just briefly going to introduce that document. Can we scroll it up a little bit, please? So the Main Staff here is informing about the activities of our opponents, that in Pazaric, Tarcin, and Bjelasnica, the Operations Group Pazaric was active, which is comprised of seven brigades, and that from the town of Sarajevo, also, they're acting -- then in the third paragraph, it says: "These forces are planning to carry out a joint assault operation, with the objective of linking up the Bjelasnica-Trnovo-Gorazde road." And the beginning of the operation is announced for the mid-September of this year. Can we scroll up the page a little bit? I have to read slower, but I don't have time. And it says here: "It is to be expected that there will be artillery and mortar support, the equivalent of two batteries' strength. En masse, strong sabotage groups are expected to be infiltrated into the rear, and the disposition of our forces in order to inflict losses, cause panic, cut off communications, take dominant elevations, with the objective of preventing manoeuvring and the supply of our forces, and to create conditions to break up and destroy the cut-off units." Can we have the next page, please? Well, actually, we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is a document of the 16th of September. The Main Staff is informing about its operative and intelligence data. Do you recall that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time was preparing these actions that are being referred to by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, or, rather, do you remember this actually being implemented shortly after the 16th of September?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I do actually remember this operation, no, not the way it's been written up here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender the document, please? This is one in line, and it is going to lead up to the crisis of the 22nd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I've been -- first of all, it's not a matter of the authenticity of the document, as the Court is aware. In terms of its contextualisation and the options of admission at this time, at least under MFI conditions versus Bar Table, it may be the case under the circumstances that have arisen here, and given the answer of the witness, that the Court may get considerably more illumination from a Bar Table submission than was permitted here. On the other hand, it may be that in the context of the accused's overall questioning, it may be suitable for admission and contextualisation under these circumstances. But given the answer of the witness thus far, I would probably encourage the Court to consider this more appropriate for Bar Table submission, with the contextualisation offered by that process.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, I'll hear you before we make a decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: Definitely, this witness does not have to know or be familiar with each document, but the topic that the document deals with is something that is touched upon in his statement as well as in the events that ensued. From day to day, the situation was developing, and this is one of the documents that would need to be tendered. We already have a lot of documents that we are going to tender through the Bar Table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be added to your list of documents to be tendered through Bar Table. We will not admit this at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 16871. 16871. Could I ask the parties to look at this letter by General Gvero, which is sent through the office of the UNMO at Pale. And he explains in paragraph 2 that: "On the 18th of September, 1994, at 1730 hours, Muslim forces started with simultaneous assaults from Sarajevo onto the RS Army positions on the confrontation line," the line of conflict: "The village of Mrkovici, the village of Faletici, Lapisnica, Trebevic ..." And then it says: "They used 82- and 120-millimetre mortars and are firing from Bascarsija and in front of the Assembly building ..." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This first paragraph, could you please look at it, and do you agree that the Muslim Army began this offensive of theirs on the 18th of September, just as this letter sent to the UNPROFOR Sarajevo Command indicates? General, do you remember that the offensive began that General Gvero's letter is informing your command about? Do you remember the offensive beginning in the way that is described here?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the letter now and refreshing my memory. I'm vaguely remembering that there was an offensive like this. If I could see the second page, if that's possible. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's all right, look at page 2, but there's nothing of importance on it. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the question to the witness, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina began their offensive just like it is written in this letter by General Gvero? The general said that he vaguely recalls this offensive, and now we're going to shed some light on this offensive using UNPROFOR documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And if I recall the chronology correctly, the general asked if it was possible to see page 2. Then the accused said he wanted to tender the document, I think before the opportunity was provided, but I think we probably ended up with a request to see the remainder of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the general looked at the second page, which is very short. And now the general can answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sir, I do vaguely remember the incident. As to the specific details of how it started, that's unclear. I do remember that there was an offensive around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D773, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 09662. This is a 65 ter number: 09662.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could I please ask you to look at this UNPROFOR document, your command's document, dated the 18th of September. Actually, it speaks about the 18th of September. And at the top, yes, it is dated the 18th of September. Does this document indicate that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out an attack towards the north, towards Mrkovici? It says "Mekovici" here. Do you recall where the village of Mrkovici is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall where the actual village is, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to recollect -- help you to recollect by telling you that you have to reach Mrkovici by going through Spicasta Stijena, north-east of Sarajevo, would that help you a little bit to remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would -- a map would just be helpful, just to orient me to the ground here. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are going to deal with Spicasta Stijena, then we will show you that. But I would like you to look at the contents of the document and to confirm that the Muslim side fired 58 projectiles, that it violated the exclusion zone, and that the Serbs only later decided to retaliate from Poljine, from the place where the Serbian artillery was collected.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give a minute here and I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we collapse this B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, the report is clear, how many rounds were fired. In the report, it's clear on what happened at this point in time. I don't -- I don't doubt the details of the report, as it's come out of our headquarters. And as to the violation of the total exclusion zone, if it was, we would have definitely protested against the Muslims for this action.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please. And that deals with precisely what you were talking about just now. I'm afraid that this is too far. Well, in English, it's the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You saw, on the first page, that you got in touch with both of the warring parties; first, with the 1st Corps of the B and H Army, and then -- actually, and you asked them to stop the attack. Then you got in touch with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that correct? So you were absolutely aware that they had launched an operation and that they had violated the zone, and then after a certain period of restraint, we retaliated; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, what we did was, as written there in the second-last paragraph, contacted the BiH Corps, asking them to stop, and requesting the Serbians not to reply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you agree that from 1715 hours, when the attack started, until 1815 or 1820 hours, the Serbian side did not retaliate, and then after an hour they retaliated from the Poljine sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct from the report that is being submitted here, that I'm reading right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree, General, sir, that this is a sufficient period of restraint, and that you could clearly see here who started the attack and who had the right to respond?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see from the report who initiated the attack, and what I could see is the other side defending themselves. And after that, we would have to sort of talk about where the -- those rounds were going in to. So somebody is attacking, somebody is defending.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But when the exclusion zone was violated, in that case is it significant who violated it and who responded; who was the one who acted and who reacted? Does that have any significance in this matter?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both parties, if they violated the total exclusion zone, would be held accountable, and we would protest against both parties if they violated that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's stay with this case. General, did the Serbs violate this agreement here or, pursuant to the agreement, did they have the right to take back their own weapons and defend themselves? Did that not -- was that not stated in the agreement, that they had the right to take back their weapons and defend themselves in the event of a violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, I would have to re-read the agreement, which -- I'm not going to put 10-plus years back in the memory here. I'd have to re-read it to answer your question specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you should take my word for it. The Prosecution and the Trial Chamber have seen it. But, in any case, can we look at the following page. Until we call up the document: You will see that we did have the right to do that, and it seems that somebody in UNPROFOR forgot about that right of ours. This is how our command characterised this action or, actually, the reasons for the attack started by the Muslim Army: They had two objectives; to block the road, and the second reason was to give President Izetbegovic a significant argument at the time when he's negotiating in the United States, the lifting of the embargo, pushing the Serbs to make a fault by shooting on the city. The Bosnians also fired diversion shots in the south-eastern outskirts of the city in BP 93-58 Sector with the possible objective of simulating an attack, and so on and so forth, along the road to Pale. Do you recall that warning from the Main Staff to the corps commands that this would occur, and did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It would be "how your command characterised this action."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document from the Sarajevo Command, so this would have been our position and our assessment of the objectives of this action on this day. I will agree with what has been written here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the previous page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, would you say that this was a proportionate response by the Serbs? Can you please look at this and tell me whether it was a restraint and a proportionate response by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my assessment, that would be a fairly proportionate response from 1810 to 1840.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this document admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D774.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look briefly at D717. It's an agreement on the weapon collection points. It's already in evidence, but we need to refresh the general's memory of the document, itself. So it's D717. I apologise to the OTP for this document not being on our list, but since it's already in evidence, I think it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this first page? Although you were absent at the time when the agreement was concluded, but can you confirm this is the first page of the agreement? Actually, the agreement, itself, is an annex which is on page 4. Therefore, can we have page 4 now, please. It's entitled "Protocol of Understanding Between the Civilian/Military Representatives of the Republic of Srpska and UNPROFOR." Can we please look at item 1, which reads: "In the event that UNPROFOR withdraws for any reason ...," et cetera - everybody can read it - and the last sentence says: "In the event of a Muslim attack on Serbs which UNPROFOR is not able either to prevent or stop immediately, the VRS Army reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence." Do you agree that an hour of restraint and the suffering of the consequences was enough grounds for us to implement Article 1, or item 1, from this agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess the issue I have is in the beginning it says: "In the event that UNPROFOR withdraws for any reason from mutually agreed sites ..." I'm not sure how -- I would need to get some interpretation how that relates to the bottom, where: "... BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence." So in that paragraph, to answer your question, UNPROFOR, in the case of the 18th of September, didn't withdraw. It was a Muslim attack. So I think UNPROFOR's position at the time would have been that because UNPROFOR didn't interfere with this attack and that it didn't withdraw, it would probably have some issue with -- about pulling weapons out of the weapon collecting points. But that's just my interpretation of that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We both agree that UNPROFOR did not either prevent or stop the attack, nor did they warn or threaten the Muslim side by NATO bombing; is that correct? Please have an understanding for my desire to get a yes-or-no answer from you, because I would like to finalise this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR did try to warn and stop the Muslim attack, after they started it. I can't give you a yes-or-no answer. It's just, you know, the document I read had us protesting the Muslims for the attack and asking the Serbs to withhold their fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the general gave his answer as far as he could, so you can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The position of the Defence is that UNPROFOR issued a warning only after the Serb response, but before that they did nothing to prevent or stop the attack. Had we not defended ourselves, there would not have been any termination of the attack. But let's move on. Can I have now 1D02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that a question, whether -- you can answer the first part of his comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The attack was neither prevented nor stopped by the UNPROFOR. You may have given or issued a protest, but you did nothing to prevent it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did nothing to prevent it, but we tried to stop it after it commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you failed to stop it until the Serbs responded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not stop the attack. The Serbs fired back in response to the Muslims. Our engagement was verbal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have document 1D02553. Let's just look at it briefly in order to see what the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is writing in its report. It's dated the 19th. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps is informing the Main Staff about an attack which took place at 1730, saying that the Muslim forces commenced an attack from Sarajevo at the VRS positions at Mrkovici, Faletici, et cetera. They are using 82- and 120-millimetre mortars, and the attack lasted until 2030 hours. We had -- we had some dead soldiers and wounded soldiers. The attack from Sarajevo was aimed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please read slowly and indicate which paragraph he is reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, please. The interpreters couldn't interpret what you said from: "We had some dead soldiers and wounded soldiers." But you can put your question. You don't have to read out all these details. You can summarise and then put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is citing exactly the same reasons here, stating that the objective of this attack is to provoke a response from us and then to lay blame on us. And then later on it says that General Rose had accused the Muslim side that they were the first who caused conflict in Sarajevo, and he threatened both parties and requested them to immediately suspend the conflict, and scheduled a meeting with representatives of the warring parties. So we see here that the purpose and the aim of this attack is exactly the same. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D775, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D02554. This is dated the 21st of September, 1994, i.e., one day before the NATO operation. I'm going to read only the first sentence under the heading "Enemy." The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is writing this to the Main Staff of the VRS. It says: "Any agreements or warning from General Rose are futile when it comes to the Muslim forces. Fire is being opened from the exclusion zone by using artillery pieces exceeding the calibre of 12.7, targeting our positions and villages also within the exclusion zone." Can we now look at the next page, please. Item 8, "Conclusions and anticipation or prediction." "The enemy is not giving up on provocations and attacks on all defence lines within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. In spite of the warning issued by General Rose, today, from the urban part of Sarajevo under Muslim control and from the exclusion zone, fire was opened from mortars and PATs at Mrkovici. In the forthcoming day, the Muslims will continue to use military, political, and psychological and propaganda means in order to exert pressure on the Serbian forces in order to provoke extensive conflicts that would be conducive to lifting the blockade of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, General, do you agree that this is proof that the Muslims were firing from the exclusion zone at our positions and our villages within the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims were firing from the exclusion zone, and that activity was protested by Rose and by my boss against the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they bombed by NATO for what they did?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't, because there were no targets to bomb. But they were protested by NATO -- not by NATO, but by the UN for their actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D776, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they were not bombed, was that because UNPROFOR did not send such a request, or was it that they did request it but NATO refused to comply?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN never made a request to NATO to bomb the Muslims while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were the Serbs bombed on the 22nd of September?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall. I believe that they were bombed around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that, according to this agreement and the protocol on weapons collection, we were fully entitled, in the aftermath of an attack that could not be prevented or stopped, to retrieve our weapons and defend ourselves?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer is: No, I do not agree with that, in accordance with the agreement that I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, what were we entitled to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were entitled to defend yourselves and use the weapons systems that you had. But the weapons in the weapon collecting points were there to control what was in the exclusion zone and outside, in accordance with the agreement, and I think you had other options to address this issue, other than what was -- what was taken on the ground. You asked for my opinion, and I've given it to you. And I think there was enough resources on the Serbian side to adequately defend themselves against a very small attack in a very small frontage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, General, they attacked on many lines, and they were using the artillery with a calibre larger than 12.7 millimetres. Do you think we could really counter the attack by mortars, 82 and 120 millimetres, PATs, and other weapons? So -- with the weapons that we had at our disposal? So is the agreement still in force if one of the parties violates it? I'm afraid the translation was not good. Were we able to defend ourselves with infantry weapons from the attacks from artillery with the calibre exceeding 12.7 millimetres, which were banned, actually? And is an agreement still alive if one of the parties violates it? Is then the other party obliged to still adhere to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your first question, Were you able to defend yourselves, I think, you know, based on my experience, there was enough weapons systems and people around the area, not the weapons that were in weapon collecting points, that you had sufficient resources to defend yourselves on that -- in that attack. As to the question, Is the agreement still alive after one party violates it, I would say, yes, and it behooves the parties to go back and to negotiate and to reinforce the agreement, as we had done repeatedly with sniping -- anti-sniping agreements, to keep a lid on this situation for the benefit of the innocent people in the whole region, both Muslim and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, was it possible for us to have weapons in excess of 12.7 millimetres in order to defend ourselves? I can tell you that we couldn't, because you would have bombed them, as you did on the 22nd of September with the tank. This is explicitly stated in the protocol, but then why were we bombed on the 22nd of September, and why did this disrupt our relations with you? Were we an outlawed party and fair game to be shot at, whereas the other side was free to do as they pleased?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this is another example of a compound question. Which one do you want the general to attempt to answer, and in which order? One question at a time is more than enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And speaking for myself, Mr. Karadzic, I don't see any relevance. The trial is not why NATO bombed, so I think you exhausted the topic sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, if that's the position of the Bench. I just wanted the general to help us understand why we were bombed and what our position was, and the issue of our relations with the United Nations, because everything depended on the involvement and the interference of the UN in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General? Count 11 in the indictment, the entire count deals with our conduct after massive attacks on our positions. The crisis between your side and our side started long before that, and the crisis was exacerbated by the interference of UNPROFOR and NATO bombardment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for your information, General, Count 11 refers to taking hostages of UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I just have the question repeated, which one they want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, General, I have great sympathy with you. Dr. Karadzic is doing it again. If you want a specific answer, you've got to ask a specific and focused question. Making a speech and adding questions throughout is not helpful for the witness, and it's certainly not helpful for the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, and thank you for these well-intentioned suggestions, but I have a problem with the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, General, do you agree that our relationship greatly depended on the actions or impunitive actions undertaken by the other side in the conflict and on NATO actions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our relationship depended on the actions of all three parties, being the Muslims, the Serbs, and the UN, working together. NATO was a consequence based on a request from the UN, but the UN was the actual requesting agency. So I would agree that our relationship depended on the actions of all parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have document 65 ter 09691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Tieger, having followed the lines of questioning, in particular regarding the combat or attack in the middle of September, the Chamber is of the view that we have sufficient basis now to admit 1D2623, which is one of the Main Staff documents dated 16th of September, in terms of contextualisation. So we'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at this regular report of the UN, dated the 17th November 1994. Do you recognise this regular out-going fax sent by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the cover sheet. I would like to see the details, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that UNPROFOR here reports about a series of incidents that took place on the 16th and 17th of November? Between 2300 and 2330 on the 16th of November, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina fired four rounds from the area bounded by the Presidency, the residency, and Kosevo Hospital. The round impacted in the area of Rajlovac and Slavino Brdo. Do you agree that Rajlovac and Slavino Brdo are Serb-held territories or, rather, Serb settlements in the town?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acknowledge the report, and the areas that you mentioned were Serb controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on the 17th, from early dawn, i.e., from 7.15 until 8.00, you can see that artillery rounds, 105 millimetres, were fired by the BH Army. Three impacted inside the compound of the electrical transformer station, nine rounds landed in a civilian area. Two civilians were injured, one seriously. The firing point was in Goviniste. Do you agree that this was again the Serbian area being targeted and that water supply for the entire city of Sarajevo depended on this electrical transformer station?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the rounds were fired from the Muslim side into a Serbian area. I'm not -- I can't remember if that transformer controlled water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 3, the Army of Republika Srpska, the Bosnian Serbs, replied with 120 mortar from the weapon collection point at Ilidza. Six rounds landed in Kovacici, near the HQ of the 4th Brigade. Do you remember that there was the 4th Brigade in Hrasnica under the Command of Fikret Revenjak [phoen], and that this reference to Kovacici actually refers to the HQ of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the brigade and the commander. I just can't remember the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And paragraph 4: "At 800 hours, the Serbian side replied at Ilidza. Three rounds landed in Hrasnica, near the rear of the HQ of the 4th Brigade." Do you agree that the UNPROFOR here identified that target?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR identified the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 5 states that the building of the Presidency was attacked from a Maljutka, and two 82-millimetre rounds. They hit the south wall of the building, and that this was a response to fire the previous night which came from the vicinity of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to read the document and listen to you at the same time. I would agree that the rounds were hit -- the Presidency was hit, and probably in connection with the attack the night before. That would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now on this page that we can see, UNPROFOR is asking for meetings to be held with Mladic, another meeting with Hajrulahovic, and that the issue of opening heavy weaponry fire from the town should be opened, which violates the exclusion zone, and then the check-point system for the collection of weapons should cease immediately and there should be an agreement with more stricter rules. And it says: "Any future abuse of this system could result in military action." They're probably thinking of NATO here. General, sir, do you agree that the Serbs reached for their weapons, which is what we can see on the basis of these documents, only after they were attacked, doing so a few hours after the fact? [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, to answer your question, reached for their weapons after the attacks, in contravention of the weapon collecting point agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last item here says additional measures are going to be requested, which have already been agreed in principle, for the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. Are you aware that the Serbian side was always in favour of the demilitarisation of Sarajevo and for placing Sarajevo under the administration of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that position, but that's not to say that my boss wasn't. I just wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D778.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you to understand the need of the Defence to be more specific about the statements and positions so that we could separate those for which there is evidence from those which are based on impressions. I don't want you to understand as if I were attacking the United Nations or any person within the United Nations. I would just like us to differentiate between an impression -- between information from the Bosnian side and what has been established beyond any doubt by the United Nations. I would like you now to focus on sniper activity in Sarajevo. Do you recall that there were screens between positions of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those screens or sea cans, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that these screens could protect civilians and others in Muslim territory from Serb fire, but not from fire from Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because they were designed to protect from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the intention and did you put in any efforts to erect any more of such barricades and to increase this safety measure against infantry fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a concerted effort to erect barricades to increase safety throughout the city, where they were needed, not just simply on Sniper Alley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the authorities in the Muslim part of Sarajevo did not agree, and that this effort to erect barricades was halted? You can look at page 24 of your statement, if you like: [In English] "The sector tried to improve the situation as regards the barriers by putting more."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Sometimes the city wanted it; sometimes they didn't."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't dispute that. And in every case, as I recall, the safety of the citizens was paramount, and we would do what we thought was right to protect citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you have an explanation why the town -- or the administration of the Muslim part of Sarajevo did not follow you in these efforts, why they were against the erection of these barriers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is my explanation acceptable to you, that they needed to have their citizens victimised in order to keep attention on themselves and draw the sympathies of the international community?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an explanation. It's a pretty sad commentary, but I -- I don't ever recall asking the Muslims why they didn't -- what was behind the fact that they didn't want certain barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that the so-called Sniper Alley is a limited area, stretching some 200 to 300 metres from Marin Dvor to the Marsal Tito Barracks?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that in your observations about General Galic and General Milosevic, you did not consider them to be unintelligent and irrational people? You considered them to be quite intelligent people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, can you tell us who benefitted, politically, from the events in that Sniper Alley area from Marin Dvor to the Marsal Tito Barracks? Who benefitted, politically, from the things that happened in that area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we conclude, then, that two generals who are not stupid or mad would not deliberately and consciously allow, never mind order, something that would harm not only the other side, but would harm the Serbian side quite considerably as well? If you are not able to say, then I am going to withdraw the question. But you decide.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would acknowledge that both the corps commanders demonstrated a degree of professionalism and intelligence, experience, control over their forces. And that said, they did control the actions of what happened there, which included sniping, based on my assessment of how they were running their operations. So I guess I'm left with a question, myself, is: Why would somebody who demonstrated command and control would allow sniping in this area that would actually benefit the other side, politically, from a tactical military action? I mean, they were not dumb people, but dumb things happened; that they would go after non-combatants, and, you know, the results were for the world to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct you said that -- that in the criminal legal sense, investigations conducted against civilians, Bosnians, Herzegovinians, people regardless of their faith, were conducted by local police forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question. UNPROFOR did its investigation, as well as the local police. That's what he said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR investigated incidents against UNPROFOR, not against civilians; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an attempt to circumvent the Court's reminder that this series of questions was asked and answered. In fact, the questions were posed in precisely this order, and this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness can answer the last question of the accused. Could you answer that question again: UNPROFOR investigated incidents against UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We investigated all incidents, not just against UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have this material, the documents relating to these investigations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the documents in my possession. I know I read a couple of documents since I've been here relating to some of the incidents, but the UN would have made a report for -- we made daily reports on incidents like this, and they were submitted up the chain. So there's a record in the UN archives somewhere of the time that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I would be repeating myself. When I asked you about the criminal investigations, you said that this was something that you did not do, that this was something that was done by the local police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct; we would investigate, but if there was a crime committed, that would be done by the proper authorities, and our investigation would end with just ascertaining the facts and if a violation had been created by one of the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the forces there were quite close, and that frequently, near the Vrbanja Bridge and around the Jewish cemetery, the proximity of the forces resulted in frequent exchanges of fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it time for a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If it is convenient, we'll have a break. But, Mr. Karadzic, you'll have about three-quarters of an hour to conclude your cross-examination after the break. We'll resume --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I hope that the Trial Chamber will review its decisions. Really, a vast number of facts has been touched upon, and statements by this esteemed witness -- can only be clarified with this esteemed witness, not with anyone else. So I'm just trying to clarify with him whether something is established, or its second-hand information, or it's just an impression. I cannot verify this except on the basis of his statement and with this witness, and there is a number of things that need to be specified in more detail. So I hope you will not miss the opportunity to permit the Defence to be quite precise about a number of issues that will not be able to be specified with any other witness other than this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as we made it clear before, we'll assess, at the end of your cross-examination, whether you would be allowed further time for your cross-examination, but it depends upon the efficiency of your cross-examination as well as the remaining issues, considering all the circumstances. We'll consider it after the 45 minutes which is still remaining and which can be used usefully and efficiently by you. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you were not in a position to check on the Serb side, regarding Sniper Alley, whether there was visibility or a line of vision between the place that the fire was suspected to be coming from and the place of the incident?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, we were not in a position to check because the Serbs did not give us freedom of movement, although my general did visit at least one building on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the buildings along the front-line were frequently used for attacks or for defence -- or, rather, there were holes on the walls of those buildings that you were able to observe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, do you agree that this did not mean that the hole indicated a sniper's nest, but that it could also have been used for infantry weapons during the defence of the line or in attack?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been used for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the use of silencers also made it difficult to identify the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you something about the trams. Who decided whether trams should run and whether it was safe enough for tram traffic to proceed? More precisely, were you asked for your position on this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city authorities decided when the trams would run and not run, and I'm not sure if we were ever asked our opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 40 in e-court. This is your answer on this topic from your amalgamated statement. Your answer begins with the words: "I don't ever recall ..." [In English] "I don't ever recall them coming to us, asking us for advice on running the tram."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this answer of yours implies the position that you were constantly being asked to do something and that, before that, they complained about increased firing on the trams?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that, yeah, sometimes they would ask us to do something when the sniping was increasing, but, by the same token, we were also putting up passive barriers. But I would not abrogate the responsibilities of the local officials to do the same thing themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From your answer, it can be concluded or it can be made as a conclusion, which is also our finding, that firing at trams, in a way, was also a way to exert pressure on the United Nations to do something; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you observed that Muratovic and others, but particularly Muratovic, was trying to get something for nothing, as you put it; in other words, that they were trying to take some advantage from your mediation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that Muratovic tried to get as much out of the UN as he could, with the engagements that we had with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have P435. This will help us remind ourselves of this specific topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that the Vrbanja Bridge from the church at Marin Dvor is about 70 or 80 metres away?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that would be -- that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if a tram were to be hit at Marin Dvor, near the church, that would be 70, 80 metres, but if it were hit near the Marsal Tito Barracks, that would be around 300 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your -- your distances, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have page 2, page 10 in English, in this document. [In English] "Assessment."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I kindly ask you to focus on this paragraph, which begins "Assessment," which reads: "Although the number of firing incidents decreased, tension is likely to remain at an elevated level following the shooting incidents by uncontrolled elements at the airport and against the tram." Do you agree that the United Nations established that there was fire opened by uncontrolled elements?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a degree of uncontrolled elements, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the previous page in English. Can you please scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This passage, which starts: "A tram travelling ...," speaks about an event of 27th February 1995. As a result, a woman, who appeared here as a witness, was wounded. Can we scroll down more to see where you established -- only I am not sure whether this the right page, but it says: "The tram service was stopped after this incident. Both sides participated in the same period in an armed conflict 300 metres away, in the area of the Vrbanja Bridge (BP 912589)." Yes, this is -- this is the passage in the middle of the screen. So it is clearly confirmed here by your observers that they knew very well that there was exchange of fire 300 metres away, in the area of the Vrbanja Bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report clearly states what happened in this case, where the assessment is that the casualty was probably as a result of the engagement by the two warring factions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now have P1773. P1773. Let's first identify the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is an UNPROFOR report, it's Sarajevo Sector, which contains a proposal for a meeting to be held concerning sniper activities? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 3 in the English version, please. "The main problem now is that there is more and more victims from lost bullets, as exchanges of fire are increasing on the confrontation line close to inhabited areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was an assessment of your command, which was to serve as the basis for the forthcoming meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an assessment of -- produced by this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you recall that these buildings around the Sniper Alley are to the north from the River Miljacka, and that these buildings were also suitable to be used for combat operations, and that they were, in fact, used for those purposes, such as Unis skyscraper, the government building, and other such buildings? Do you recall knowing that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that these buildings were used for combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now deal in more detail with the issue of aerial bombs. In our conversation, you were kind enough to say that you don't remember any aerial bomb landing in an inhabited or an industrial zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said I don't remember it landing in an industrial zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember it landing in a residential area? And if you do, where, exactly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back to refer to my previous testimony. I do recall that aerial bombs were used, and I'd have to go back to refresh where we noted where they landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, let me ask you this: In your opinion, what impact an aerial bomb of 100 to 250 kilograms can have on a building made of bricks?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A 250-kilogram bomb landing on a concrete or brick building, it might punch a hole in it. Might. If it's on an apartment block, it would probably do little to no damage. If it was a house that had brick and mortar, it would probably have more of an effect, but it's a pretty wide question you're asking me, because buildings run the gamut. But 250 kilograms against an apartment building, little to no damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would happen if it landed on the ground? What would the consequences be?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Landing on the ground, it would probably have a greater impact, in the sense of just sending up shrapnel and fragments to the radius of whatever that size bomb is, and that would be determined by whatever -- the size of the warhead and the type of ground that it hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But without a doubt, it would create a large crater. 250 kilograms equals --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't catch the figure of TNT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your last digit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A 250-kilogram aerial bomb has about 100 kilograms of TNT. Do you agree with that, and do you agree that it would create a considerably large crater?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a big bomb that would create a big hole in the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know and do you agree that the aerial bombs were propelled by rocket motors that had their performances and range tables, on the basis of which it was possible to establish their range and their precision of engaging targets?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that the rocket motors used had some fairly detailed specifics for range. When you strap on the rocket onto another -- the bomb itself, the characteristics of the rocket motors themselves will have changed because of the aerodynamics, and that's something that I would have to read the report on how effective -- or what's the result when you strap on two different items together when you launch it. So rocket motors, by themselves, are probably pretty well defined, but when you add that to a bomb, that gives you a different set of parameters. So that would be -- that would be something that I would ask more questions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree if this was tested and fired, then these performances can be identified and established precisely?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If tested and fired, yes, you could determine the performance. "Precisely" would be a function of the warhead, whether or not it was guided or just ballistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I kindly ask you now -- or, rather, to remind you, and for that I would need P1782. P1782 refers to Hrasnica, which is something that you would surely recall. This is a report of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps relating to attacks on Hrasnica. This is already in evidence. And one can see in passage 1 that the Muslims were launching attacks from Hrasnica against Famos factory, that two women and a civilian were wounded. And further on, we see that there were other casualties. And can we now look at the next page. Can I ask you to look at item 2, entitled "Our Forces." Please scroll up. And it says here that: "Our forces responded to enemy fire from infantry weapons." And then it says: "... one 250-kilogram aerial bomb was launched at the centre of Hrasnica." Is this consistent with what you commented on with respect to this Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I recall stating that I saw this document, and it looks like a 250-pound -- kilogram aerial bomb was launched at the centre of an urban centre called Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that this had been prepared two or three days before to be engaged in targeting Hrasnica, and that this was mentioned in another document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's a reference to a particular document. I think it would be more appropriate to show that. And I say that because I'm not -- based on the evidence we've heard thus far, I'm not sure what the accused is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he can put the question. And if the general cannot confirm it, he can show the document then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, if I understand it, it's the 4th Brigade that Fikret was commanding, was in Hrasnica. Is that what you're alluding to, the other document you showed me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This report relates to the fire, but two days -- or one day before that, General Milosevic ordered this launching. I can call up this document, it's in evidence, but let me ask you this: Did that go -- did that go without saying that this bomb was actually to be launched at a civilian area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the document that's in front of me right now, it seems to indicate that an aerial bomb was launched at the center of a town called Hrasnica, which would suggest to me it's a civilian town. It said "launch," I think earlier: "... launch at the center -- launch at the center of Hrasnica." And the Muslims claimed that the Luna rocket landed. So I'm just taking from what it says here, that he's reporting he launched it and it landed in the middle of a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why we need 1D2622. Before this document appears, let me ask you this: Do you agree there was a certain kind of understanding or agreement between commanders that if a superior commander issues certain orders to his subordinate commander, that they both understand and know very well which targets they're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no, no. If a commander issues an order to a subordinate to engage a target, the definition of that target should be clearly spelled out for the subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if they had prior agreement and were -- the subordinate commands were briefed about the targets, does the full name of the target have to be repeated over and over again?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer is, yes, it's a common professional understanding and procedural issue that when you issue orders to engage a target, you are specific in the target you want to engage, i.e., the white building at grid 123456 or latitude and longitude. You specify exactly where that target is that you want to engage. Using generic names, in anything that I've ever done in 30 years, is not detailed enough for subordinates to execute on. In fact, we actually put target numbers on commonly repeated targets that are used over and over again. We will actually give them a specific code to expedite the description or the talking about. We'll give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at this. The 4th Motorised Brigade, this is a report by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, or, rather, an order for further actions, and it says: "In front of our forces from the 82nd Division ..." That is, before the 1st Corps was reorganised and divided into three divisions. Look at the one-but-last bullet point. It says: "The 4th Motorised Brigade, 4.500 strong." And the last sentence says: "The disposition of the said brigade is as follows:" Can I please have the next page. Next page, please: "The 4th Motorised Brigade, with its command post at the post office in Hrasnica, made up of four motorised battalions and military police companies, IDC Black Panthers, IDC Fikro's specials," and they are defending a certain area. Then: "The 4th Motorised Battalion has mortars, 120 millimetres in Vukovi, 105 millimetres in Radeljevaca, 82 millimetres in Vrhovi Sector, and again 82 millimetres in Bijela Kosa Sector." So this is the deployment within Hrasnica, itself. And the last sentence says that they are deployed in some other areas as well. So would you agree that all of this, particularly the post office, were the places where their forces were deployed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document, it would appear that the brigade headquarters was in the post office.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification, Mr. Tieger? Yes, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D779, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D2625, please. Just briefly, let us identify this document, which says that the municipality of Hrasnica -- or, rather, Ilidza, and the post office are on Halid-bega Hrasnice Street number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take the accuracy of the document. If that's where it says the address is, I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have document 2626, which will show us where exactly this Halid-bega Hrasnice Street is located. 1D2626. Can you please enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the map of the Hrasnica neighbourhood and that Halid-bega Hrasnica Street is in the very center of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we need to tender these two documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need translation? Can I see the previous document again, 1D2625.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are postal units or post offices in Hrasnica where the command HQ was, was on Halid-bega Hrasnica Street, and then the map shows the location of the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you need a translation of this document or this will do as it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not the translation that immediately comes to mind as an issue, Your Honour, but several steps that I'm uncertain of here, including the relationship, temporally, between whatever this document indicates and where the post office was at the time. I -- I mean, first of all, a translation would probably make it easier down the road, but of greater concern is: What's the nature of this document, the source of this document in particular, and what's its relationship temporally between the period we're talking about and the period of time referred to in this document? And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the Defence will admit that this is a very contemporaneous or a recent document. And then, as such, well, its probative value will depend upon the other corroborating evidence. So, as such, there would be no problem in not admitting that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's been referred to in court, we know what it says now, but it's clear that whatever significance can be attributed to it, it's going to -- we're going to have to know whatever -- whether the post office remained in the same place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it, both of them. The first one will be marked for identification, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be MFI D780, and the map will be Exhibit D781.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D2621, please, so that we can have a more complete overview of what is in Hrasnica. This is an archival list of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. It has its own ERN number at the top. Can we now look at the next page, please. The title is "Data on the Enemy in the Hrasnica Sector." And then it says: "4th Motorised Brigade (Vitez)." And then there is the sector of responsibility and the formation, the command, motorised battalion, logistics battalion, military police company, Special Unit Fikro, Special Unit Crni Labudovi, Black Swans, POV Britve, MAD Igman, and a signals unit. Under "Command," it says "Prevljak, Fikret," whom you met, and then his other associates: "The Command of the 4th Brigade is located in the premises of the new post office in Hrasnica and most probably will be relocated to Sokolovic Kolonija. The brigade numbers 4.500 soldiers." First of all, I wanted to help the general, to remind him what was the armed force located in Hrasnica, and ask him whether they knew of the existence of this brigade and its deployment or disposition in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew of the brigade. The actual deployment of the brigade would have been known by the French Battalion in the area. That was not the level of detail that I was conversant in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to remind you, I mean, 4.500 soldiers, 4th Motorised Battalion, 2nd Motorised Battalion -- can we look at the next page, please. 3rd Battalion, 4th Battalion. All of them were in different locations. Logistics battalion, military police company, Special Unit Fikro, and we can see all the things that they had: PATS, PAMs, mortars. Can we please look at the next page. Six Special Unit Black Panthers, and then Britve, then Igman, which also has a 152-millimetre Howitzer, five pieces, and 105 millimetres, five of them. And it also has a 130-millimetre cannon. It's deployed as support for the 4th Brigade, 5th Motorised Brigade, and the 102nd. So it has five 102-millimetre mortar -- 152-millimetre mortar and five 105-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that Hrasnica was literally teeming from the armed force of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see is a list of units. I wouldn't expect any commander to put them so much together that they would create a target of -- a target-rich environment. I would have had those forces spread out throughout the entire area. And I can't tell from this document, you know, where -- exactly where they were located. It just tells me what was -- what was in the 4th Brigade, and some details, but I would have to see the translation to see what exactly this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, General, sir, you would not need to compare yourself with Fikret, of whom you said in one of your statements that he was a scoundrel; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see what I said about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take my word for it. You said that he was very bad and disobedient. Anyway, can we look at the next page. In this document it is said what they had. And here is a table showing us what things looked like. The 4th Motorised Brigade had 4.500 soldiers, three tanks, five armoured personnel carriers, one Vidra, eight 120-millimetre mortars, 19 82-millimetre mortars --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're simply wasting your time. If the general cannot confirm any of this, you're just simply wasting your time. What's the point of reading this document in such a detailed manner? Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you recall, in your dealings with Fikret, that you called him some kind of a renegade, and you said that he wasn't obedient enough to Karavelic, that he was a commander in Hrasnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that Fikret was difficult for Karavelic and that he seemed to report to a higher authority than the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're not denying. You don't have any elements to be able to deny that this is the firing power of the 4th Motorised Brigade that was under the command of that man; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been, but they did not share their -- this document or their combat power with us. They kept it hidden from us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to ask Mr. Tieger again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was looking earlier for any references to the date of this document, the nature of this document, and I didn't hear any, so I'm at a loss at this point to advise the Court that I have no issues concerning its authenticity and reliability and that sort of -- in that sense. And, of course, the witness was not in a position to offer much more about the document, other than it contained a reference to someone he had referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And he confirmed the existence of 4th Motorised Brigade in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, which I think had been done previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to add, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just that this document was obviously received by the OTP investigators from the archives of the Ministry of Republika Srpska, that it was obtained later, and that it speaks about events about which the general is familiar. It is important to us to see whether Hrasnica was a civilian zone or whether there were preconditions there for military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You know well by now what matters when admitting certain documents. It's not an issue whether it is received by the Prosecution or not. As you indicate, this is a document originating from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. But Mr. Tieger raised the issue, when this was produced and by whom, and on what basis, but you didn't give an indication as to those questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is stated in the document. We're going to look at it. This is 1994/1995. That is the year. The name of the command to whom the archival material belongs, Sarajevo Romanija Corps, keep permanently. This relates to 1994/1995. The situation in this sector of the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, which bordered on Hrasnica, and its armed forces there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is probably a report covering the period from 1994/1995. But you still are not aware of when this document was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Given that this has an ERN number and it was produced to the Prosecution, how do you expect us to know that? I think it's for the Prosecutor to tell us, from their own records, when that document was produced to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's be realistic about this. I'm presented in court with -- we get, if we're lucky, these documents immediately before cross-examination commences.
