Now I have a document in B/C/S. I think I've reasonably asked for sufficient information to respond to the Court's inquiry about admissibility. Now, we do have some additional information provided by the accused, which seems to me could have been provided at the time it was tendered, as we were going through it. It's not clear to me, on the basis of the document, what 1994 through 1995 represents. I can't tell, reading it, if it's supposed to be a contemporaneous account of forces, if it's a retrospective -- contemporaneous retrospective, or if it's a retrospective created far later. I think all of that does impact on the weight to be given this document. I also think the Defence is aware that the Prosecution has not attempted at all, during the course of this case, to impose any formalistic barriers to the admissibility of documents, but just reasonable ones. And I think the questions I've posed in this context have been quite reasonable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist? On the first page, it says it comes from 1994/1995, so it was created or stems from 1994/1995 and was archived later by someone. It says here "originates from 1994/1995," so the document was created in 1994/1995, if that is of any help. There is a large set of documents, but for this witness, for this topic, we picked this situation in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- sorry to interrupt the Court's deliberations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- but since I think it began with an inquiry to me, and I posed certain questions in an effort to respond: While I have -- well, I obviously have questions about the overall utility of this document in the context the broad issue in this case, and I have some questions about the weight to be given the document, in light of some of my earlier remarks. I don't have the same issues that I raised before some of the additional information was provided that I did earlier, so I'm -- I would not object to the admission of this document, in light of the additional information. It has been to be MFI'd, of course, and I again underscore my concerns about the weight to be given the document, but in trying to be consistent with our previous -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but which is what the additional -- what is the additional information you've got in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When I first stood, we hadn't -- we hadn't heard anything about the timing of the document, what it purported, when it purported to have been collected, when it purported to have been assembled and made available. Now, I think it's been -- if I understood the responses correctly, all of which are dependent upon interpretations which are not available to me, it seemed to be a roughly contemporaneous account of a previous period. Now, that previous period, it seems to me, undercuts the weight to be given the document. But if the accused's position is that he wants the Court to consider it with respect to whatever weight the Court might accord it, in light of that -- in light of the fact that it seems to focus largely on whatever the 1994 through 1995 period is and whenever the transition of that period occurs, however early in the year 1995, then I accept that -- if I understood, again, the answers of the accused, that it's a document that was -- that demonstrates on -- or indicates on its face it was roughly contemporaneously prepared by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Now, if that's not the case, and it may not be because I've been receiving this on the fly through the explanations, our position might be different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may -- before you make your decision, if I may explain. The previous document, MFI D779, precisely repeats the number of soldiers, 4.500, as well as the deployment of the force. This document was drafted more or less at the same time and is quite consistent with this document which was archived later, but its origin is in 1994, just like Mr. Tieger said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as regards the MFI'd 779, we can understand in what context the document was produced and what it refers to. But in relation to this document, we are not satisfied on what basis this document was produced, and we need to know that in order to properly assess the weight and probative value of this document. The part which the witness has confirmed has already been in evidence, so we don't need to -- we don't feel the need to admit this. And you'll have another opportunity to tender this. So we'll not admit this. Mr. Karadzic, I noted that your time's up, so we need to discuss whether or not to extend your time to cross-examine the general. So could you briefly tell us -- tell the Chamber, without going into detail or going into merit, what areas you have to still cover and how much time you need to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I actually need just one more document in relation to this order, and then all that remains is to cover the question of the demilitarised zone in Igman, which the general touched upon, and then to specify, in the general's statements and also in the transcript, what he meant. These are a number of things that the Defence needs to cover in more detail, because if they were left as they are, they could be a source of major danger for the Defence. Of course, we are counting on our position being made easier if the documents we wish to submit through the Bar Table are accepted. So we would like to use a substantial part of the next session to clarify these matters, and that would bring us, then, to the end for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If I may be permitted one hopefully quick observation, and it's simply this: This is a pattern that I think we've seen repeatedly, where the usefulness of much of the time that preceded the request for additional information -- for additional time that comes at the end, plus a specification of the uses to which that time would be put, is -- where there's a disparity between -- or at least an arguable disparity between the two. Now, in this case, it's difficult to tell from the vague submissions the accused made about what he wants to further explore, how valuable that might be. What I do know is if the accused was requesting time to explore some of the areas that he used his valuable time for earlier, I don't think the Court would be receptive to that, and I'm including such matters as the lengthy inquiries, and the black-marketeering, and other matters that occurred in the end, plus a fairly extensive commentary, plus the over-elaboration of certain areas that could be explored through cross-examination far more quickly. Now, I leave it to the Court as to what it wants to do, but I just fear that we're at risk of developing an approach where the accused feels reasonably free to use his time as he wishes in the early phases because he has some level of confidence that if he leaves until the end topics he considers important, the Court will feel compelled to expand his time, even though he hasn't heeded the admonition to use his time more usefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with the observation by Mr. Tieger. As I indicated to you, you should have prioritised your questions. You spent much of your time on the issues which have been, in the view of the Chamber, only of limited value. The Chamber will give you half an hour to conclude the cross-examination of General Fraser. It's up to you, how you use the remaining time. We'll have a break after that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one word? From the point of view of the Defence, even the smallest question, which can serve as the basis for a conviction, is a major question. That is why we don't know which questions are not important. We've seen, from the practice of this Tribunal, that even a tiny question can serve as a ground for conviction -- for a conviction. Thank you for the additional time granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 65 ter 10644. I am asking the other side not to be cross about this. It's not on the list, but it arises from what we were talking about, and it stems from the possible lack of understanding about the order of General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is two days before the air-bomb was launched. The 4th of April, two days before it was launched. Can we look at the next page, please. The next page, if we can look at it both in the English and the Serbian. And can you please look at the tasks: "Prevent the enemy infantry from advancing." That's the first part. The second part is: "Prevent the enemy swift breakthrough." Then, continuing: "Neutralise the activity of enemy artillery and mortars, and immediately, upon taking up firing positions, proceed to make fire adjustment with the battery's main artillery pieces and direct fire artillery pieces upon the first detected target." General, do you agree that that order, which went into effect a day or two later, is in a kind of continuity in relation to this order?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order looks -- it's clear to me what the commander is asking you to do. This is very clear: "Make fire adjustments with the batteries main artillery pieces and direct fire artillery pieces upon the first detected target." That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the order, issued a day or two later in light of this, was clear to the subordinate commander; he knew very well what his commander was asking him to do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who signed this order was very clear, what he wanted, and his subordinate should be fairly clear what he was looking for. If you go back up to the first paragraph, it says: "Preparing barrage fire Alpha along the --" if I can fill in that blank -- "axis and barrage fire Bravo along the village and other village axis." That's fairly clear, where he wants fire to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this document admitted into evidence, please ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you remember the crisis that emerged in relation to the demilitarised zone at Igman. So in that context, can we have 1D2609. Are you familiar with this layout of the separation line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. I've never seen it portrayed on a map like this before, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that one can see here that Sarajevo, through the airport, is connected with the wider area of Igman and Bjelasnica, as shown in this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in the summer of 1993, we captured Igman and Bjelasnica, which became the source of the crisis because only then was it considered that Sarajevo was under blockade, and that was the reason for NATO to issue its ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at that time we reached an agreement with the United Nations for Igman and Bjelasnica to be converted into demilitarised zones and to be handed over to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then when you were already there, that is, on 6th of October, 1994, you noticed a Bosnian Army unit passing through the demilitarised zone and subsequently killing, according to you, 19, but unfortunately we know that 20 members of the medical unit were killed.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that incident, and we protested strongly against the Muslims for the operation going through the DMZ and for the fact that they killed medical personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the capturing of the demilitarised zone by the Muslims generated a long-lasting crisis in terms of our relations with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and UNPROFOR alike?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, and we were in constant dialogue with the Muslims to have them respect the terms of the DMZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that both General Rose and General Gobillard, and everybody from the UN, invested enormous efforts in an attempt to force the Muslim Army to abandon the DMZ and let the United Nations take charge, and that it took a long time before that happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the French Battalion was even compelled to use force and bulldozers, and that in the course of that operation, an attack was launched by the BH Army, or, rather, Fikret's brigade, against the French Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark on this map, by using a pen, the demilitarised zone that we handed over, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't, at this stage of the game, remember that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that entire units of the 1st Corps were going in and out of Sarajevo through this territory that was linking Sarajevo and Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this map be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll admit it as Exhibit D783.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now specify in more detail a number of things mentioned in your statement. On page 11, do you remember making reference to the existence of red dossiers that you did not have access to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it's noted in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that on page 13 it is written that all the reports were first returned to the sector, and then those that were more sensitive or had media implications were passed on to the command for Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you explain to us why and in what sense the sensitivity existed, as well as media implications, that could have constituted a reason for concealing such reports from the public?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on page 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the Serbian, page 13. I believe it's page 13 in English as well, and the title is "Shelling."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two issues, Your Honour. First of all, I think the page reference in English should be 12. But more importantly, I think there's some confusion between the amalgamated statement, to which the witness may be referring at the moment, and the -- and just to make sure I'm right about that -- and to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is referring to his 1997 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, and I don't think the witness -- I'm not certain, at any rate, that the witness was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is the amalgamated statement. Yes, it's possible that it's the 1997 statement and the portion relating to the shelling. [In English] "All reports came back." [Interpretation] "All reports came back."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what way these reports were sensitive, and what kind of media implications they had, and why was this material treated differently?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, nothing was hidden or -- it's a normal procedure that reports from subordinates, coming up to the sector, would be vetted to meet the information requirements for our higher headquarters, and it would be consolidated up -- into reports that would be sent up to BH Command. Any reports that would have any media implications, i.e., that were going to generate interest in the media, would be certainly put into those reports to alert the commanders and information staff that what -- what they'd have to deal with. But at no stage in the game would I suggest, and it's not stated in here, that we hid anything. In fact, we're the UN, everything was in fact open. That's why we didn't have intelligence sections, we just had information sections, because we were not conducting operations against any of the warring factions. And as it says there, the information officers of both Sector and BH Command were well aware of the situations and how to be prepared to brief the media each morning, because there was a media scrum, and the media had freedom of movement over there so they could find out a lot of information themselves, which would come up in the form of questions to our information officers each day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Karadzic, you are not minded to tender this statement, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just want to specify, in more detail, some views and opinions, and this is helpful to the Defence. But, however, we do not need to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking you, if it is not admitted, what's the point of clarifying some passage of this, but it's up to you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall mentioning that on the 7th of May, everything exploded in Sarajevo, and that the 5th Bihac Corps was in the process of attacking? This is stated on page 0055-5103 from your 1997 statement, and I think it is also contained in your amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 23, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this crisis that involved the 5th Corps and Bihac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this crisis arose, first and foremost, because the forces from the protected area of Bihac invaded a large territory which was purely Serbian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Corps came out of the Bihac area and attacked into the Serbian-held territory up in the north-west corner of Bosnia, correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have, please, 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the accused please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic .

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2610. Can we please scroll down a bit more so that we can see the legend. We need to go up a little bit more to see -- it's not possible. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this full line was the separation line on the 23rd October 1994, and the dotted line is from the 1st of November, 1994, and this is the area captured by the 5th Corps over the course of one week? Is that correct? Can the general please be shown the whole map so that he can see the dates attached to these two lines in the legend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the origin of this map, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this question has already been asked, so pardon me, but this is the CIA map, one from the entire collection of maps produced on a daily basis and depicting the deployment of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it may also be helpful to know the direct providence of this map, Your Honour. I mean, I understand that's the accused's position on the basic source, but where -- whether this purports to be an original, which I presume it doesn't, where the copy of this map came from, did it come from some publication, from -- was it retrieved from some kind of archive, how is it that it is understood to be derived from a particular source? That would be extremely helpful. I mean, there's a lot of information on the map, as the Court can see, that purports to be more than geographic information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't have it so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you hand it over to the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has already been mentioned here. There's a whole set that we received courtesy of the United States of America. Some maps contained the name of the publisher, and the publisher was identified as the CIA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the front-line as of the 23rd of October and of the 1st of November. Is this consistent with what the Muslim Army achieved, in terms of capturing territory during that week?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is consistent with what I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now -- but before that, can we have this map admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit D784.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D2611, please. If we face the same problem with the legend, I would kindly ask that the general be given a hard copy. Can you scroll down, please, and also can you deliver the hard copy to the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, General, let's try and see if we can find the legend. This depicts the counter-offensive launched by the Serbian forces. The legend is not completely visible, but can you tell me, does this correspond to what you knew about the Serbian counter-offensive against Bihac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does jive with what I remember of the counter-offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this map admitted into evidence? And I need this document, containing an order issued by General Delic in one sentence, to be placed on the ELMO. Is this map going to be admitted into evidence? It's the map showing the counter-offensive, whereas the previous one showed the offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the witness's answer, in a manner similar to the previous document, I presume it's going to be admitted. However, I trust that the Defence will be co-operative with the Prosecution as we attempt to obtain a bit more information to identify with greater clarity the providence of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would expect the Defence to co-operate with you. That will be admitted as Exhibit D785. I note the time. Have you almost concluded or are there --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nearly. Thank you for your understanding concerning the map. And can we please now have this document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order of General Rasim Delic, dated the 16th November 1994, issued at the time of the Serbian counter-offensive. Allow me to read it: "Intensifying of combat operations. Order to the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 7th Corps. "Bearing in mind an extremely complex situation prevailing in the 5th Corps, and with a view to tying up as many aggressor forces as possible, intensify combat operations to the maximum in your area of responsibility." General, do you remember that during our counter-offensive against Bihac, the whole of Bosnia was on fire, all the front-lines were active?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With the consent of the Prosecution, can we tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document I need to be shown on the ELMO, and I would like the general simply to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this general? Is that General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell from that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But it says in the text that it is General Karavelic. Can you please scroll down a bit. "Five offensives launched by the 1st Corps this year." The highlighted portion says: "This is testified to in the best way by our five offensives and one defensive launched during this year." General, do you agree that it was the 1st Corps who initiated fighting in Sarajevo, and that this interview confirmed that in the course of that year, they launched five offensives and only one defensive operation? So that was the 1st Corps deployed in the area of Sarajevo. Do you recall that the United Nations thought, as well, that it was them who initiated the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, because -- I mean, in part because we're at a disadvantage, in light of the absence of translation, I was -- I tried to be fairly attentive to the relationship between the question posed, the representations made about what the document states, and what was read out and translated. And it seems to me that there's an expansion of what was translated from the article and what the article purports to represent. The quote was: "Five offensives launched by the 1st Corps this year." An expansion into the accused's version of where that took place, and so on. And in fairness to the witness, if a question like that is going to be posed, then I think -- and if there's any hope of getting any kind of meaningful answer from the witness on that issue, then I think he has to be given the opportunity to know what's -- what General Karavelic purportedly said in this article, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Despite that and albeit the compounded question was on five lines, and then I think the general can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to the number of 1st Corps offensives -- offensives they conducted, I can't tell you, off the top of my head. Was it five? But if anything was done in -- you know, in contravention of any of the rules and regulations and agreements we had, we would have just protested against him as much as we would have done against the other side. That's -- that's all I can tell you. Is the number five? I don't know. We dealt with each case individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whether it was the 1st Corps that initiated the offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not matter what the unit was. It only mattered what side violated what, and we would go after that side, given the agreements we were trying to uphold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Tieger, I take it you have some questions for your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. I think not more than 10 to 15 minutes is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break now, 25 minutes. We'll resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask if this interview can be tendered for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You know the position of the Chamber. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. The accused asked you, at page 25 of today's transcript, General, about screens that were set up to protect civilians from sniping by the Bosnian Serb forces. Now, I wanted to ask you a couple of questions about those screens or barriers, General. First of all, even after those screens were set up, did the Anti-Sniping Task Force continue its efforts or cease its efforts?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The efforts were continuous throughout, even before, during, and after the screen emplacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that a reflection of the view that the screens alone would not be sufficient to eliminate completely sniping against civilians by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Screens had a positive impact, but it just would move the problem elsewhere. The snipers would go elsewhere until they found a position where they can gauge targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact -- and, in fact, was there a continuation of sniping against civilians by the Bosnian Serb forces after the establishment and placement of the screens, the protective screens?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, today, at page 34, you were asked some questions about Exhibit P435, and your attention was focused on a portion of the document relating to an incident on February 27th, 1995. And perhaps we can call up P435. And just to remind you, General, there were two aspects of this document that were brought to your attention by the accused. One --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just make a brief intervention. Is this question a leading one if you say, Were the forces of Bosnian Serbs firing at civilians, without evidence, without an investigation? I'm afraid that then this is a leading question. What is being provided as evidence that that is so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The general has answered the question already, and it follows the general's answer that the Anti-Sniping Task Force efforts were continuous. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, one technical problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, I just wanted to -- I was about to recall two areas of focus about P435 asked by the accused, and one was with respect to a tram shooting, and the other with respect to an armed conflict in the area of Vrbanja Bridge. I take it you recall that discussion generally?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The accused did not note to you, and I want to bring your attention to it, that this was the subject of considerable discussion with you during the course of your testimony during the Dragomir Milosevic case. In fact, it consumes quite a number of pages of that transcript, during which it appears this document was made available to you for a period of time and you were given an opportunity to review it. And you had an opportunity to review at that time, as reflected in your amalgamated statement at pages, approximately, 46 through 50, not only the portions brought to your attention by the accused, but also an additional portion of P435 at page 23, and that's paragraph H of that exhibit, which refers to a sniping incident against civilians on the tram. And, General, if I can -- in light of all the information you had an opportunity to review during the course of your testimony during the Milosevic case, let me ask you to turn your attention to what you said beginning at page 49 of your amalgamated statement. You were asked, toward the bottom of the page, whether it could be concluded from the report that there was an exchange of fire, and that as a consequence, the tram was shot. "The consequence of this exchange of fire, is that something that could be inferred from this report without really going into the details?" And then you responded: "I also read in the report that, in fact, there appears almost two things happening here. This was an engagement at a bridge, and there appears to have been some sort of sniping activity on the tram." If we continue on to the -- and you say: "So we could actually have two incidents actually being reported in one paragraph. That's how I'm -- I'm actually referring from this report." Then continuing on to page 50, you note the deliberate nature of sniper action. The question is: "So out of this report, do you read that it was a deliberate -- a deliberate action?" You answer: "What I read from this is, as it appears from paragraph H, the tram was sniped at." And you continue to say, based on your review of the totality of the document: "There was no direct correlation made from there that the fighting there actually impacted on the tram. In fact, this tells me -- gives me, for detail, from that to say I think there were two things happening in the same time-period, a fight at Vrbanja and sniping against a tram. That's what I'm getting out of this report." And that's at page 50. And you reaffirm the same thing in the immediately subsequent answer, as you can see as you continue down the page. And you say: "Well, again having read the more details, again, I would infer from this that while there may have been fighting going on at Vrbanja Bridge, someone in this area might have directly targeted and sniped at the tram at the same time, because it -- again, when I put those two pieces together, that's the kind of picture I'm getting when I read this report." And, General, having now had the opportunity to see your amalgamated statement, and reflecting on your previous testimony and the opportunity at that time to see more excerpts from the document, do you stand by that answer in your -- by those answers in your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before that, Mr. Robinson, can I see the passage which refers to both sides being involved in a fire-fight 300 metres away in the area of the Vrbanja Bridge in that exhibit? What page was it? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the reference was to page 9 of the document, if I'm not mistaken. There's also a similar reference at page 2. And I think, if I'm correct, that the reference was made to page 2 and page 9 today, earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, this is a very leading examination and I think it's really an improper re-direct examination to have led the witness in this manner. This is not the way to refresh your witness's recollection, if his recollection needed refreshing in the first place. Secondly, I just point out it's a small point -- it's a small point, but we had a lot English -- reading of English text by Mr. Tieger that could have been read by the witness by himself and all of us could have read it, and you frequently admonish Mr. Karadzic abut that, and I couldn't let it pass that this is the same kind of thing that you say is a waste of time when it's being done by Dr. Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that we admitted his amalgamated statements into evidence, I don't think Mr. Tieger's question was leading, and we'll just -- since you admitted it's a small question, I will not address that issue. General, could you answer the question, having heard all these questions and submissions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand by the -- what my statement said here in the abbreviated -- in the document, this one [indicates], my abbreviated submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think "amalgamated" is the term we use here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, "amalgamated statement," I stand by that because you have to read the whole report and not just a couple lines to get the entire sense, and we went through that in some detail in that other trial, and I stand by what I said then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And then one last area of inquiry. You were asked yesterday, at pages 8093 through 8094, about an issue I wanted to address. You had testified, and you testified yesterday, about the targeting of civilian areas by the Bosnian Serbs, and about the firing of weapons which were incapable of distinguishing between military and civilian objects. And in response, the accused confronted you with a portion of a statement by Bosnian 1st Corps Commander Karavelic, in which Karavelic made some observations, and your attention was brought to a portion of the statement where Karavelic made some observations about the Sarajevo Romanija Corps use of standard types of barrage fire, waves of fire, protective fire, selective fire, and concentrated fire. And then the accused said to you that, There is nothing illegal in this characterisation, is there? Do you recall that, General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me, therefore, show you another part of Mr. Karavelic's report which the accused did not show you. And if we can call up Exhibit 11377, please, and turn to page 16 of the English, page 17 of the B/C/S. Sorry, you may not have heard that. 11377. You may be calling it a P number. I think that's a 65 ter number, isn't it? 65 ter, yeah. And if we can highlight, please, the -- about the fourth paragraph from the bottom, which begins: "Throughout the war ..." This is the portion of General Karavelic's statement that you were not shown and that I wanted to bring to your attention: "Throughout the war, the Serb forces made no distinction between military and civilian targets. Anything that moved, including civilian pedestrians, came under fire. Hospitals, schools, and historical buildings received direct artillery, tank and mortar fire on a regular basis, while houses, apartments and gathering places, such as markets and water lines, would be shelled without seeming pattern. Nobody knew when and where a shell would hit, so every place was dangerous." Now, first of all, General, using the accused's formulation, is that a characterisation of Bosnian Serb shelling that indicates something illegal?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, is that generally consistent with what you observed or were made aware of during your own tour of duty in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It distinctly resembles the pattern that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Nothing further, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put two questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In response to what questions from Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness, the general, was misled in relation to the incident of the 27th of February. He was not told or shown that the fire that wounded Alma Cehajic was a burst of fire. The first burst of fire missed the tram, the second burst of fire hit the tram, so perhaps his position would have been different in relation to sniper activity. The first part has to do with Karavelic's statement, but the second part, actually, is part of an expert testimony. So the question is: Does the general know that we are talking about a burst of fire here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's for the Chamber to assess the evidence later on. We'll not allow you to put that question. That concludes your evidence, General Fraser. On behalf of the Bench and the Tribunal as a whole, I thank you for your coming all the way to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have about half an hour to conclude for today, and I think we can continue. The witness is waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I was advised that, because of protective measures in effect, we need to break for five minutes in order to bring the witness in. So we'll break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 6.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for your inconveniences, and I'd like to thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can I say that your oath is still in effect. Therefore, you don't have to repeat your solemn declaration. And you will be cross-examined by the accused, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would immediately like to move to an incident that you processed. This is incident number 8 from the F list. This is the sniper firing at the tram on the 19th of June, 1994. Is this an incident which happened at Marin Dvor, in front of St. Joseph's Church?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the tram was moving from Bascarsija towards Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many persons were wounded? Is this number known?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't be certain, but I think it's three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking because the indictment states "four," so it would be of assistance if we knew the precise number. Can we look at 1D02584 now, please. And can we ask the witness to help us to mark the place of the incident? Can we zoom in on this part, the part where it says "Marin Dvor," and can we go a little bit towards the east. Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The upper part. Further up, further up. Do you like to zoom in further, Mr. Karadzic, or this is sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is sufficient, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this part of town, the part that we're seeing on this map?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Marin Dvor, from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can I ask you to mark on the map the place of the incident? Can you please mark the church and the other buildings that you need to in order to specify the incident site?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more or less here [marks], and this is where the church is, from what I can see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to mark the precise incident site, because this area is a little bit too big.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the intersection where the accident -- or the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The intersection is towards the Branimira Cosica Street. What is the name of that street now?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that was its name at the time. I would know it by its new name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please mark with the number 1 the incident site?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 1. Can you please mark the place where the incident occurred with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, very well. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that you did not manage to establish exactly who fired, but in your findings, you assumed that this was done by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We established the direction from which the bullet came, and I couldn't tell you more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the direction here on this map?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. It's more or less like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you make it longer, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, like that, thank you. And can you mark that line, the direction, with the number 2, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the OHR building, and would you agree that that is the former Unioninvest building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you circle that place and mark it with the number 3, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where the line of separation was here on the left bank of the Miljacka River?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- well, which is the left and which is the right side? This is the left side [indicates]. As far as I know, it was along the Vilsonovo Setaliste, along the Miljacka, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can we agree that each bank was controlled by one of the sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But here, near the bridge, are you able to say where the line of separation was here in relation to the direction where the bullet came from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you precisely, but I, again, would say that it was along the Vilsonovo Setaliste Street, along the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the right bank, are you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on the left side, I think somewhere, is where Skenderija is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate that, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that it was here [indicates] somewhere, as far as I can find my way on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that place with the number 4, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As it is indicated here, then, the Unioninvest building would be under the control of the Serbian side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D2584, please. And, first of all, can we tender this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to put your initials and the date.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My initials and my date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. First, can you confirm that this is the incident location? That's number 1. Number 2 is the direction the bullet came from. Number 3 is the Unioninvest building. And number 4 is, in your opinion, the area or the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can you please put your initials or signature here and the date.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the basis of these assumptions, you drew a conclusion about the trajectory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D2584 now, please -- 1D02434. 1D02434.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a Sarajevan, is this a photograph well known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the incident site on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear your answer, Mr. Vidovic. Did you say "yes" to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that I am familiar with this place. This is the crossroads at Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this photograph was taken from in front of the St. Joseph's Church?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to mark on this map the incident location?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the tram tracks, this part here [marks]. I'm not able to say exactly which part of the intersection that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, can you mark that with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The incident site is marked with the number 1. Can you mark the street that goes towards the Vrbanja Bridge now, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more or less here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought if you can mark it length-wise. This is the intersection. Would you agree that Turcianska is at the back of the photograph that goes towards the Strahimira [phoen] Kranjcevica Street, the second street goes towards the Dobrinja -- no, the Vrbanja Bridge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this street goes towards the Vrbanja Bridge, like this [marks].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could you please delete the circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you please mark with the number 2 the line indicating the street that leads to the Vrbanja bridge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you recognise this hill up there? Which hill is that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the hill, but I know the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know where the line of separation is between the two armies here?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be at the end of the street leading to the Vrbanja Bridge, so it would be at the Vrbanja Bridge along Vilsonovo Setaliste Street, along the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to concentrate at this edge, where the trees are. Do you see the chapel there and the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on that part a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will lose the markings if we move the map. Do you know where the Jewish cemetery is? Do you see a chapel up there along -- right next to this green tree?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can mark it again, but let's -- why don't we zoom in further and then try to mark it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the chapel now right in the -- right next to the foliage of the tree?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it's somewhere here [indicates]. I can see it, more or less, here through the foliage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you move it to the left a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to push a certain button in order to mark it. Could you wait a minute, Mr. Vidovic. So we mark again the place of the incident around the tram rail. Put number 1. And number 2 for the road leading to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you please mark the chapel now and the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mark it with the number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is this building, this layered building in the forefront, this large building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you put the number 4 on the building? Anywhere, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you know who was in this building? Who held this Assembly building during the war, under whose control was it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under the control of the B and H Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to now look -- if you're familiar with the area, to look at the eastern boundary of the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it would be somewhere in this circle that I drew, but I'm not sure, and it's not very easy to see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put your signature and the date on the photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let the photograph remain on the monitor for a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I will ask you this: If I were to tell you that in the eastern part in relation to the Jewish cemetery, there were positions of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army, would you say if you knew that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know where these positions would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the western boundary of the Jewish cemetery, there were Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the western boundary of the Jewish cemetery from here?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- due to the tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us who was controlling the slope of this hill during the war, the slope that we are looking at now in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say exactly. As far as I know, this part was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, this part towards Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to mark the positions that you know were held by the Army of Republika Srpska? Can you use red to mark this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just speculate or assume, but I don't know where their positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you just mark that in red?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness has said he doesn't know what the positions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vidovic said he can't. We'll admit this as Exhibit D788.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation was not correct. I actually asked for this document to be tendered and not -- but, all right, very well. Can we now look at the previous map one more time, 1D2584.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the Jewish cemetery here, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Urjandedina to the east, and to the west, Locatelli. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Serbs were on the western boundary of the Jewish cemetery, the Muslims were on the eastern boundary, and the rest was no-man's land?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about the no-man's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can't say anything about the lines here, then, can you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can just speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, we are not going to tender this. We are not going to be marking anything here. Can we look at the photograph again, an unmarked one, 1D02 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest of the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, now it's back to me. Can we just leave the photograph as it is, without zooming in. Can we show it as it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, can I ask you to tell us, please, from where could you fire on these tram tracks? Was it possible to fire from the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible to fire from the Kapela section?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could, yes, according to this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to fire from the area to the left of the chapel, from the east side of the chapel on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that this entire slope that looks on the intersection was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the Unioninvest building, which is now the OHR building, was controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the whole time, except for at the beginning of the war in 1992, would that be acceptable to you, including the petrol pump that we saw and the OHR building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when we look at this photograph, would you be able to, only on the basis of the sound that you hear, to decipher that the firing -- or the origin of the fire was the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. That was the last question, but the interpreters couldn't hear your answer because both the interpretation of the question and your answer were overlapping. So tomorrow, please put a pause between the question and the answer. What was your answer, Mr. Vidovic, to the last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's it for today. We'll adjourn for today and resume tomorrow at 2.15. Have a nice evening, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
